opus-5.5.text:
I'd say world models are promising but still early, maybe somewhere between a research direction and an engineering discipline. People mean quite different things by the term, so it helps to separate them.

One version is the generative, video-style world model: you train on huge amounts of video and the model learns to predict what comes next, sometimes conditioned on actions. These have improved dramatically. The visual fidelity is impressive, and you see some emergent sense of physics, like object permanence and rough dynamics. But under the hood they're often still pattern-matching on appearance rather than holding a consistent, causal model of the world. Run them long enough, or push them into unusual situations, and things drift: objects morph, physics gets violated, consistency breaks down.

The other version is more abstract: a model that captures the latent structure of how the world works, so an agent can plan, imagine counterfactuals and reason about the consequences of its actions. That's the part I think matters most for AGI, and it's also the least mature. We don't yet have a clean recipe for learning representations that are compact, causal and useful for planning across many domains at once.

There's also an interesting question about language models. They clearly learn some kind of world model implicitly from text. They know a lot about how things work, how people behave and what follows from what. But it's patchy, and it isn't grounded in perception or action the way a child's understanding is. So one big open question is how much grounding you actually need. Can you get there by combining language, video and interaction data at scale, or do you need fundamentally new architectures and objectives?

So my overall assessment is that world models are almost certainly a necessary ingredient. Any system we'd call generally intelligent needs to predict and simulate the world in order to plan and act reliably. But I don't think they're sufficient on their own, and we're not yet at the point where they're robust or general enough. The bottlenecks are things like long-horizon consistency, data with real action and feedback signals, evaluation (how do you even measure whether a world model is "correct"?), and integrating the world model with reasoning and decision-making.

The exciting part is that the pieces are converging. Scaling, multimodal pretraining, robotics data and simulation are all feeding into each other. I'd expect a lot of progress in the next few years, but I'd be cautious about anyone claiming world models alone are a solved path to AGI.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls world models early and expects progress in the next few years, but does not suggest that they may still be at a stage comparable to early single-GPU foundation-model pretraining five years from now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say world models are promising but still early, and I think it's worth separating what we mean by the term before judging maturity.

In the narrow sense, a world model is a system that learns the dynamics of an environment, so it can predict what happens next and plan against that prediction. In the broad sense, people now use it to mean something like an internal, generative simulation of reality, the kind of thing a model would need to reason about physics, causality, and consequences without being told explicitly. The first sense is fairly mature. We've had good results in games and in robotics simulation for years, and video generation models have shown that you can learn a surprising amount of physical intuition purely from pixels. The second sense is where the AGI claim lives, and that part is much less proven.

My honest assessment is that we're at the stage where the demos are compelling and the benchmarks are weak. A model can generate a plausible video of a ball rolling off a table, but plausibility is not the same as a consistent, queryable model of the world. When you probe these systems on object permanence, counting, long-horizon consistency, or counterfactuals, they still break in ways that a child wouldn't. So the generative quality has run ahead of the structural understanding.

I also think the framing of world models "versus" large language models is a bit of a false choice. Language models already encode a lot of world knowledge, just in a lossy, text-mediated form. The interesting work right now is in combining them: grounding language models in learned simulators, using world models to give agents something to plan against, and using language as an interface for abstraction over those simulations. Whichever lab gets that integration right will probably have a stronger claim on the path to general intelligence than either camp alone.

The thing I'd watch for as a sign of real maturity is sample efficiency. Humans build world models from remarkably little data. If a system needs hundreds of millions of hours of video to learn that objects don't vanish when occluded, it's memorizing patterns rather than learning a model. When we see world models that learn new environments quickly, transfer across domains, and support reliable planning over long horizons, that's when I'd say the approach has gone from promising to foundational. We're not there yet, but the trajectory is encouraging.

r001.rationale: The response calls world models promising but early and says they are not yet foundational, but it does not suggest where they may stand five years from now or compare their development stage to early single-GPU foundation-model pretraining.

astra-6.text:
I think world models are a promising direction, but we’re still early. The key question is whether a model can predict how the world changes when you take an action, and use that prediction to make better decisions.

There’s a difference between generating a plausible video and having a model of the world that’s reliable enough for planning. A video can look convincing while getting an important causal relationship wrong. If you’re using that model to control a robot, those errors matter, and they can compound as you plan further ahead.

What I’d look for is whether these models can handle unfamiliar situations, recognize uncertainty, and improve through interaction. Can they test a prediction, learn from the result, and adapt? Those are stronger signals than visual realism alone.

So I wouldn’t say world models are a solved path to AGI. They could be an important component, but we still need to understand how to connect prediction with reasoning, action, and learning in a reliable way.

r001.rationale: The response says world models are “still early,” but it does not suggest that they may remain at that stage five years from now or compare their development to the early single-GPU pretraining era.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models are a promising direction, but they’re still at an early stage. The key question is what we mean by a world model. Predicting what happens next in a video is one version. Learning enough about how the world works to plan, take an action, and anticipate its consequences is a much stronger version.

We have systems that can generate very convincing predictions, but visual plausibility doesn’t necessarily mean they understand the underlying dynamics. If you change something in the environment, can the model predict the consequences consistently? Can it handle situations outside its training distribution? Can an agent actually use those predictions to accomplish a task?

So I would assess maturity by how useful the model is for decision-making, rather than just how realistic its outputs look. World models could be an important component of AGI, especially for learning through interaction, but I wouldn’t say we’ve established that they’re sufficient on their own.

r001.rationale: The candidate says world models are at an early stage today, but does not project their development five years ahead or compare them with the early single-GPU pretraining era.
